questions.question: What is the synchronized keyword in Java and what does it prevent?
questions.title: synchronized Keyword in Java
questions.direct_answer: The `synchronized` keyword ensures that only **one thread at a time** can execute the synchronized method or block. It prevents **race conditions** by acquiring an **intrinsic lock (monitor)** on an object before executing the code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core multithreading knowledge — synchronized is the most fundamental synchronization mechanism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what object the lock is acquired on
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the intrinsic lock concept and the difference between synchronized method vs block

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Block
How Intrinsic Locks Work
sections.content:
Every Java object has an **intrinsic lock** (also called monitor). When a thread enters a `synchronized` method or block:
1. It acquires the intrinsic lock of the specified object
2. Other threads trying to enter any `synchronized` block on the same object are BLOCKED
3. When the synchronized code exits (normally or via exception), the lock is released

For **synchronized methods**: lock is on `this`
For **static synchronized methods**: lock is on the `Class` object
For **synchronized blocks**: lock is on whatever object you specify

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The synchronized keyword ensures mutual exclusion — only one thread can execute that synchronized code at a time. It works by acquiring an intrinsic lock, sometimes called a monitor, on an object. When you mark an instance method as synchronized, the lock is acquired on 'this'. When you use a synchronized block, you specify which object to lock on. Other threads that try to enter any synchronized block on that same object have to wait — they go into the BLOCKED state. When the synchronized code exits, the lock is released and one waiting thread can proceed. The key thing synchronized prevents is the race condition where two threads read-modify-write shared state simultaneously.

Other threads that try to enter any synchronized block on the same object must wait until the lock is released.

Without synchronized, two threads can interleave their operations on shared data — reading, modifying, and writing at the same time. The result is corrupted state. synchronized serializes those operations so they can't interleave.

questions.question: What is a race condition and how does synchronized prevent it?
questions.title: Race Condition and synchronized Prevention
questions.direct_answer: A **race condition** occurs when two or more threads access and modify shared data simultaneously, producing unpredictable results. `synchronized` prevents race conditions by ensuring only one thread at a time executes the critical section that modifies shared state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can explain race conditions with a concrete example
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'two threads run at the same time' without explaining why that causes wrong results
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the read-modify-write sequence at the CPU level using the counter++ example

sections.title: Race Condition Example
Why count++ is Not Atomic
sections.content:
`count++` looks like one operation but is actually three steps:
1. **Read** count from memory → 5
2. **Increment** → 6
3. **Write** 6 back to memory

If Thread A and Thread B both read 5, both compute 6, both write 6 — the final value is 6, not 7. One increment was lost.

With `synchronized`, Thread A acquires the lock before step 1 and releases it after step 3. Thread B must wait until after step 3 to start. No interleaving happens — the result is always correct.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A race condition is when two threads interleave their operations on shared data in a way that produces wrong results. The classic example is a counter increment. count++ looks like one operation but it's actually three: read, add 1, write back. If Thread A reads count as 5 and Thread B also reads it as 5 before either writes back, both compute 6 and both write 6. The net result is 6 instead of 7 — one increment is lost. The synchronized keyword prevents this by making the entire read-modify-write sequence atomic. Only one thread can execute the synchronized block at a time, so no interleaving can happen.

beats.text: A race condition is when two or more threads interleave their operations on shared mutable state, producing incorrect results that depend on timing. The program might work correctly sometimes and fail unpredictably other times.

The thread scheduler can preempt a thread at any bytecode instruction. Operations that look like one step in Java source code — count++, balance -= x — are multiple steps at the CPU level. That gap is where another thread can sneak in.

items: Read: thread reads current value from memory.
Modify: thread computes the new value locally.
Write: thread writes the new value back to memory.
Race: if another thread reads before the first thread writes, the update is lost.

beats.text: sharp edge: Race conditions are intermittent — they might only manifest under high concurrency or specific timing. You won't see them in single-threaded tests. In your order app, a counter tracking processed orders might lose increments silently under load — you'd only notice if you compared the counter to the database count.

items: Race conditions are invisible in unit tests — they need concurrent load to manifest.
compound operations like if-then-modify are also race conditions even if each step is 'atomic'.

questions.question: What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?
questions.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block
questions.direct_answer: A **synchronized method** locks the entire method on `this` (or the Class for static). A **synchronized block** locks only a specified section of code and lets you choose the lock object. Synchronized blocks are preferred for **better performance** and **finer-grained locking**.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing you can specify a different lock object in a synchronized block
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that synchronized blocks reduce the critical section size, improving concurrency

sections.title: Synchronized Method vs Block
sections.content:
| Aspect | Synchronized Method | Synchronized Block |
|---|---|---|
| Lock object | 'this' (instance) or Class (static) | You choose any object |
| Scope | Entire method | Only the specified section |
| Performance | Locks longer than needed | Minimal critical section |
| Flexibility | Low | High |
| Readability | Simpler | More verbose |

sections.title: Synchronized Block Advantage
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The key difference is granularity. A synchronized method locks the entire method — every line, including parts that don't actually need protection. A synchronized block lets you protect only the specific lines that access shared state. So if you have a method that does 100ms of computation followed by one line that updates a shared list, using a synchronized method blocks other threads for the full 100ms. A synchronized block lets those other threads work during the 100ms and only blocks them for the one line. This reduces contention and improves throughput. Synchronized blocks also let you specify a dedicated lock object instead of always locking on 'this'.

groups.heading: Synchronized Method
groups.text: Locks the entire method on 'this' (or the Class for static). Easy to read and write, but it holds the lock for the full duration — including any non-critical computation inside the method.

groups.heading: Synchronized Block
groups.text: Locks only the specified block of code. You choose the lock object. Protects only the lines that need it — the rest of the method can run concurrently. Also lets you use a dedicated private lock object.

items: Use synchronized block when only part of the method accesses shared state — protect just that part.
Use a private lock object in blocks to prevent callers from locking on 'this' externally.

questions.question: What is deadlock in Java and how can it occur?
questions.title: Deadlock in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Deadlock** is a situation where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock that another holds. Thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2; Thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1 — neither can proceed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of deadlock as the main pitfall of synchronized programming
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing deadlock vaguely without a concrete example
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the two-lock example and explain the lock ordering prevention technique

sections.title: Classic Deadlock Example
Deadlock Prevention
sections.content:
Prevention techniques:
1. **Lock ordering** — always acquire locks in the same order: always lock1 before lock2. Both threads agree on the order.
2. **Try-lock with timeout** — use `ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout)` and give up if can't acquire
3. **Avoid nested locks** — minimize situations where you hold one lock and acquire another
4. **Reduce lock scope** — use synchronized blocks, not whole methods
5. **Use higher-level concurrency utilities** — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `ReentrantLock`, etc.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Deadlock happens when two threads are each waiting for a lock that the other holds — a circular wait. The classic example: Thread A locks object 1 and then tries to lock object 2. Thread B locks object 2 and then tries to lock object 1. Both are blocked forever. The most common prevention technique is lock ordering — always acquire multiple locks in the same predefined order. If both threads agree to always acquire lock1 before lock2, the circular wait can never happen. The other option is using ReentrantLock.tryLock() with a timeout, so if you can't get the lock, you back off and retry instead of waiting forever.

beats.text: Deadlock happens when two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs. Thread A holds lock1 and waits for lock2. Thread B holds lock2 and waits for lock1. Neither can proceed. The threads are stuck forever — the only resolution is a restart.

Deadlock is an emergent property of nested locking. Each individual synchronized block looks fine in isolation, but the combination of two threads acquiring the same locks in different orders creates a cycle that can never resolve.

items: Mutual exclusion: locks can only be held by one thread.
Hold and wait: threads hold one lock while waiting for another.
No preemption: locks can't be forcibly taken away.
Circular wait: Thread A waits for B's lock, Thread B waits for A's lock.

beats.text: production trap: In a banking app with transfer(accountA, accountB), Thread 1 does lock(A) then lock(B) while Thread 2 does lock(B) then lock(A). Under load, both threads can be created simultaneously with opposite account arguments — instant deadlock. The fix: always acquire locks in the same canonical order (e.g., by account ID), regardless of which direction the transfer goes.

items: Nested locks in different orders across threads is the recipe for deadlock — define and follow a global lock order.
Use ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) when you can't enforce order — at least you can back off and retry.

speakable_v2.cap: Prevent deadlock by always acquiring multiple locks in a consistent order — the circular wait can't form if threads agree on the sequence.

questions.question: What is AtomicInteger and when would you use it instead of synchronized?
questions.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized in Java
questions.direct_answer: **AtomicInteger** uses **CPU-level compare-and-swap (CAS)** operations for thread-safe counter operations without locking. It's faster than `synchronized` for single-variable operations because CAS is a non-blocking hardware instruction rather than a lock that blocks threads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern concurrency utilities beyond the basic synchronized keyword
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing AtomicInteger exists or that it uses CAS rather than locking
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the non-blocking nature of CAS and why it scales better under high contention

sections.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized
sections.content:
| Aspect | synchronized | AtomicInteger |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Lock (blocking) | CAS (non-blocking) |
| Thread block? | Yes — other threads wait | No — threads retry |
| Scope | Any code section | Single variable |
| Performance | Good for complex operations | Better for simple counters |
| Use case | Multi-variable updates | Single counter, flag |

sections.title: AtomicInteger Usage
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: AtomicInteger is from the java.util.concurrent.atomic package and it provides thread-safe operations on a single integer without using locks. It works using compare-and-swap at the CPU level — the processor atomically checks if the value is what you expect and updates it if so, otherwise retries. The advantage over synchronized is that no thread is ever blocked — they just retry the CAS operation. This makes it faster under high contention because you avoid the overhead of threads blocking and being unblocked. The limitation is it only works for single-variable operations. For updates across multiple variables, you still need synchronized or ReentrantLock.

groups.heading: synchronized
groups.text: Uses a lock — blocking. Threads that can't get the lock enter BLOCKED state. Guarantees mutual exclusion for any code section, including multi-variable updates. Overhead increases with contention.

groups.heading: AtomicInteger
groups.text: Uses CPU-level compare-and-swap (CAS). Non-blocking — if the CAS fails, the thread retries immediately. No blocking, no context switches. But only works for a single variable — can't atomically update two things at once.

items: Use AtomicInteger for counters, request counts, sequence numbers — single variable, many threads incrementing.
Use synchronized when you need to update multiple variables together as one atomic unit.

beats.text: In the order app: a request counter that all Tomcat threads increment — AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() is perfect. But a transfer that debits one account and credits another needs synchronized (or a transaction) because two variables must be updated atomically.

speakable_v2.cap: AtomicInteger is faster for single-variable operations under high concurrency — but synchronized is the right tool when multiple variables must change together.

questions.question: What is the visibility problem in multithreading and how does synchronization address it?
questions.title: Visibility Problem in Java Multithreading
questions.direct_answer: The **visibility problem** occurs when one thread's write to a shared variable is not seen by another thread due to **CPU caching**. When a thread exits a synchronized block, the JVM **flushes its cache** to main memory, guaranteeing that other threads entering a synchronized block see the latest values.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java memory model basics — why synchronized does more than just atomicity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking synchronized only prevents race conditions but not visibility issues
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java Memory Model (JMM) and the happens-before relationship

sections.title: CPU Caching and Visibility
sections.content:
Modern CPUs have local caches (L1, L2) per core. When a thread writes a variable, it may write to its CPU cache first, not immediately to main memory. Another thread on a different core may read a stale value from its own cache.

**synchronized** establishes a **happens-before** relationship:
- When Thread A releases a lock (exits synchronized), all its writes are flushed to main memory
- When Thread B acquires the same lock (enters synchronized), it reads the latest values from main memory

This means synchronized provides both **atomicity** (mutual exclusion) AND **visibility** (memory flush).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CPU caches can cause threads to see stale values
- synchronized flushes writes to main memory on lock release
- synchronized reads from main memory on lock acquisition
- This is called the happens-before relationship in the Java Memory Model
- volatile provides visibility without atomicity (simpler but limited)
- Without visibility guarantees, a busy-wait loop may never see a flag change

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The visibility problem is about CPU caches. Modern processors don't write directly to main memory — they write to a local CPU cache first for performance. If Thread A writes a value on one CPU core and Thread B reads it on another core, Thread B might read a stale cached value because the write hasn't propagated to main memory yet. The Java Memory Model guarantees that synchronized solves this: when a thread exits a synchronized block, all its writes are flushed to main memory. When another thread enters a synchronized block on the same lock, it reads fresh values from main memory. So synchronized gives you two guarantees: atomicity (mutual exclusion) and visibility (memory consistency).

beats.text: The visibility problem is when a write by Thread A isn't seen by Thread B because each CPU core has its own cache. Thread A writes a value to its cache, Thread B reads from its cache and sees a stale value. They're talking about the same variable but seeing different values.
Modern CPUs don't write directly to main memory for performance. Writes go to L1/L2 cache first. Without a memory barrier, other cores may never see those writes — or see them much later.

items: On lock release: all writes by the releasing thread are flushed to main memory.
On lock acquire: the entering thread reads fresh values from main memory.
This is the happens-before guarantee from the Java Memory Model.

beats.text: non-obvious: Without visibility guarantees, a thread running a loop like while(running) could cache the value of 'running' as true and loop forever — even after another thread sets it to false. This is a real production bug. Adding synchronized or volatile forces the thread to re-read from main memory.

items: Thinking synchronized only prevents simultaneous access — it also provides memory visibility across threads.
Without volatile or synchronized, a boolean flag change by one thread may never be seen by another.
